# Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

Two questions decide how far you can trust an AI
`r glossary("assistant")` with your code:

1. **What can it see?** Its answers are only as good as its context, and
   everything it sees has left your machine.
2. **What can it do?** An assistant that advises leaves you to filter every
   change. An `r glossary("agent")` that acts removes that filter, unless you
   put it back.

By the end you will know how to give an agent the right context, keep
confidential data out of it, and hand it routine work safely.

*⏱ ~35 minutes*


## Part A: What can the assistant see?

An assistant's answer about your data is reliable only when it has real
information: something you pasted, a file it read, or output from a command it
ran. In Block 3 you supplied that information yourself. An agent can fetch it
on its own, and everything it uses leaves your machine.


### Exercise 1: Watch what it gathers

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Watch what it gathers (8 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Start state:** your workshop repository, with a clean Git pane, and Claude
Code open in the Terminal tab with a new conversation (`/clear`).

**1. Ask without the answer-only line.** This is a Block 3 question, but this
time you let Claude Code look for itself:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
My code

  voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g)

fails with "object 'mass_post' not found". voles is read from
data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv. What is wrong?
```

**2. Read the transcript, not just the answer.** Above its reply, Claude Code
lists each action it took. When we tested this prompt, it ran a short command
such as `head -n 3 data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv` (or `Get-Content` on Windows)
**without asking**, because Claude Code treats a small set of read-only
commands like reading a file. It then named `mass_post_g` as the real column. If
it asks to run anything else, choose **No**: it can answer from the file.

**3. Name the route.** For each action in the transcript, find its route in the
diagram below: a file it read is route 2; the output of a command it ran is
route 4.

**You are done when** you can name every file or command output that reached
the model provider, and the answer names `mass_post_g`.

**If it goes wrong:** if it read more than the header, or other files, note
which: an agent reads what it judges useful, which is why the habits below
matter for confidential data.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Run the failing code in your R session, then ask only "Why did my last command
fail?" Posit Assistant already has the names and types of your objects, so it
may answer without fetching anything: that is route 3.
:::

::::
:::

::::{.callout-important}
## Working with confidential data: five habits

1. **Work on a copy.** Put a synthetic or anonymised copy in the project, and
   run the final analysis on the real data yourself, outside the agent's
   folder.
2. **Know your account.** Commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise, API) are not
   used for model training; on Pro or Max, set `/privacy-settings`. Check your
   institution's approval, ethics approval and data agreements first.
3. **Deny reads of sensitive folders** in `/permissions`, for example
   `Read(/data/confidential/**)`. It is best effort: commands can still read
   the file.
4. **Stay in Manual mode**, and refuse any command that would print records.
5. **Describe, don't show.** `names()` gives column names and `summary()` the
   shape of the data; `print()`, `glimpse()` and `str()` show actual values.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Background: tool-specific notes

There is no `.claudeignore` file, and `/sandbox` is not available on native
Windows. Posit Assistant blocks `.Renviron` and `.env` by default, and shares
the names and types of objects in your session, not their values; code it runs
can still print values.
:::
::::


### Context you hold in your head

A data file supplies column names, but not your question or your design. Your
instructor may show this with two prompts; the demonstration is below, and
you can try it yourself in *Going further*.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Instructor: demonstration

Your instructor asks a new chat:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
```

and then, in another new chat:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
```

The first gets a tour of options; the second can get a recommendation, because
the design now exists outside your head. Treat it as a proposal to check: the
primary analysis is your decision.
:::


## Part B: What can the assistant do?

The model is the same at every level below. What changes is its
`r glossary("permission mode")`: what it may do without asking. Each level is
a `r glossary("rung")` on an autonomy ladder. From rung 3 up, what changes is
which tool calls run without your approval. The self-study page
[Build your own agent in R](11k-build-an-agent.qmd) shows that approval step
in code.

| Rung | What happens | Claude Code | Posit Assistant |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Suggest | Completes the line you are typing | — | Next Edit Suggestions |
| 1. Ask | Answers; changes nothing | — (no ask mode; Block 3's answer-only line is a request) | Ask mode (`/ask`) |
| 2. Plan | Proposes steps; changes nothing until you approve | `/plan` | `/plan` |
| 3. Act, with approval | Edits files and runs commands, asking first | Manual (`default`): the workshop's starting mode | Normal mode |
| 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Some actions without asking | `acceptEdits`; `auto` (a classifier approves actions; Claude Code's own default since v2.1.283) | Auto mode (`/auto`) |
| 5. Act, unsupervised | No prompts | `bypassPermissions` | YOLO mode (`/yolo`) |

**Your starting mode.** Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in
**Manual**, although its own default is `auto` since v2.1.283; keep Manual for
confidential data. Claude Code has no ask mode, and `/plan` can still run
commands, so read any it proposes. Use rungs 0 to 3 only; the
[quick reference](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd#cc-quick-reference) has the
rest.

**Rung 3 is where routine work is safe**, for example adding a derived column
and a plot script. Three things make it safe: you start from a commit, so any
change can be reverted; every edit and command is shown to you first; and a
test checks the result, whatever the agent reports. Exercise 2 is exactly this.

:::{.callout-warning}
**Each rung up removes a moment when you would have seen the action.**
`acceptEdits` also auto-approves file commands such as `cp` and `mv`, so a `cp`
over a raw data file needs no approval. `auto` suits routine work you will test
anyway, not confidential data or anything unprotected. And an approval you
click through without reading is rung 5 with extra steps:
[Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) covers the rules that hold however tired
you are.
:::

The higher the rung, the more an agent acts on its guesses about your
conventions, which is why [Block 5](11e-instructions-skills.qmd) writes them
down.

:::{#safe-recipe .callout-note}
## The safe vibe-coding recipe

1. **Commit**, so you start from a clean Git pane.
2. **Protect the inputs:** `/permissions` shows the deny rules, or you add one.
3. **Have the checks ready:** tests in `tests/` before the agent starts.
4. **Ask** in one prompt or skill, in Manual mode, reading each approval.
5. **Run the checks:** the test suite in a fresh R session.
6. **Read the diff** in the Git pane, then commit or revert.

You will use these six steps in Blocks 7 and 9; the template ships the
protections and the tests, so most of it is checking they are there.
:::


### Exercise 2: The same task, rising autonomy

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Ask, plan, act (15 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Start state:** your workshop repository on `main`, committed and clean (the
Git pane shows no changed files). While Claude Code runs in the Terminal tab,
check its work from the R console and the Git pane
([checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work)).

**1. Plan (rung 2).** In Claude Code, type `/clear`, then:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
/plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a derived mass_change_g column (mass_post_g
minus mass_pre_g). Create a new script scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R
that plots mass_change_g by treatment_arm and saves the figure to outputs/
with ggsave(). Don't run anything; I'll check the scripts myself.
```

Before approving, check the plan names both files, leaves `data/raw/` alone
and saves the figure to `outputs/`. If anything is missing, choose **No, keep
planning** and say what to change.

**2. Act, with approval (rung 3).** Choose **Yes, manually approve edits**, so
it stays in Manual mode, and read each edit before you approve it. The
repository's `AGENTS.md` tells it to run new scripts, so it may still ask to
run `Rscript`: choose **No**, because you check the result yourself next.

**3. Check.** Click **Diff** in the Git pane for each changed file and read it
as you would a colleague's work. Then Restart R (*Session → Restart R*) and
run:

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_explore.R"))
```

One test checks `mass_change_g` really is post minus pre; the other runs the
plot script in a fresh R session and checks a figure arrived in `outputs/`.

**4. Record and commit.** Create `docs/ai-log.md`
(`usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")`) and write the first line of your
`r glossary("AI-use log")` yourself, on one line, in the form from Block 1.
Use today's date, written as YYYY-MM-DD:

```text
2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); added mass_change_g and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff
```

Commit it together with both scripts. You will add a line after each block in
which an agent works; `tests/test_ai_log.R` checks that each line has four
parts separated by semicolons, and that the dates are real and in order.

**You are done when** both tests pass, you have read every line of the diff,
and your first AI-use log line is committed.

**If it goes wrong:** select the unwanted change in the Git pane and click
**Revert**, then ask again more clearly. If you run out of time, the
`block5-done` checkpoint branch has this block's files; switch to it from the
Git pane's branch menu at the end of Block 5 if you are still behind.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stretch: reflect on the rungs

At which rung did you decide the most? Where would you have missed an unwanted
change without the diff?

**Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you
automate this again?
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Use `/plan` for step 1 and Normal mode (`/normal`) for step 2. Steps 3 and 4
are the same: the Git pane and the R console.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## At the command line

The same checks from a terminal (after `/exit`, or in a second Terminal tab):
`git status`, `git diff`, and
`Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_explore.R')"`.
:::

::::
:::


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** hand an agent a routine multi-file change at rung 3,
  **trusted because** you read every diff and a test you did not write checks
  the result.
- **Check:** the Git pane's diff after every agent action; the agent's report
  that something "still runs" is a claim until a test confirms it.
- **Reproduce:** work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change
  is a diff you can inspect or revert.
- **Record:** your AI-use log starts here, in `docs/ai-log.md`.
:::


## Check your understanding

**You paste nothing, yet Claude Code names your columns correctly. How could it
know them?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "It cannot; it must be guessing",
  answer = "It read a file in your project or ran code that printed the data, and that output entered its context",
  "It can see every file on your computer",
  "It remembers your data from a previous conversation"
))`

**In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, what does the agent do without asking?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Nothing; acceptEdits only changes how diffs are displayed",
  "Only edits to files you have named",
  answer = "It edits files and runs common file commands such as cp and mv without asking, but still asks before other shell commands",
  "Everything, including all shell commands"
))`

**Which check still works whatever rung the agent ran at?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The agent's own report that the task succeeded",
  "The approval prompts you saw while it worked",
  answer = "Reading the diff in the Git pane (or with git diff), and running the code or its tests yourself",
  "The plan the agent proposed before starting"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if
it is useful to you.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Access and cost

Plans and prices change; check before the session.

- **Claude Code** needs an Anthropic account, used through a subscription or an
  API key; see Anthropic's documentation for current options.
- **Posit Assistant** uses Posit AI Pass or your own provider key, including an
  Anthropic API key. In RStudio, providers are configured in the assistant's
  settings.
- **GitHub Copilot** bills in AI credits; check GitHub's plans page for what
  your plan includes.
- **Your institution** may have approved some of these tools and not others.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Trusting a repository's configuration

Project settings and hooks are code that runs on your machine. A cloned
repository can carry its own, so trust only repositories whose configuration
you have read.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## GitHub Copilot and the remote rung

GitHub Copilot offers the same ladder in its own surfaces. Copilot Chat on
github.com can also see files in the repository you open it from.

| Rung | GitHub Copilot |
|---|---|
| 0. Suggest | Inline suggestions |
| 1. Ask | Ask in Chat |
| 2. Plan | Plan mode in the IDE |
| 3. Act, with approval | Agent mode, approving each tool call |
| 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Agent mode with auto-approval |
| 5. Act, unsupervised | — |
| 6. Act remotely | Cloud agent |

Rung 6, the **Copilot cloud agent**, works on the repository on GitHub, in an
environment GitHub runs. It takes a task such as an issue, works on its own
branch and returns a pull request. Copilot Free includes only limited agent
features; check GitHub's plans page to see whether your plan includes the cloud
agent. The cloud agent appears in the *Going further* section of
[Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd), where its pull request meets a review
gate.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stretch: the same error at three levels of context

In three new browser chats, ask about the Exercise 1 error with more context
each time: first the error message alone; then the error plus the code; then
the error, the code and the output of `glimpse(voles)`. Only with the column
names in front of it can a chat name `mass_post_g`. Column names you never
supplied, or a famous dataset you never mentioned (`penguins`, `mtcars`), are
signs it is guessing.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Exercise: context you hold in your head

To try the demonstration above yourself, ask a new browser chat the first
prompt, then another new chat the second, and compare the answers. A data file
can supply column names and types, but not your scientific question or your
design intent.
:::
